new_statements.quote: The acoustic realisation of stress has not been measured instrumentally, so the degree to which it is realised by pitch, loudness or length is not known. ... Stress rules have been given in Williams (1980: 27) and Austin (1993a). There are exceptions, but the great majority of words are covered by these rules: 1. Long vowels are stressed, even if in adjacent syllables; e.g. dháadháa 'grandfather'. For the purposes of stress, VG and VGV sequences count as a long vowel, e.g. ngíyaningùnda '1PL-LOC'. 2. If there is no long vowel, primary stress is on the first syllable, e.g. gába 'good'. 3. Secondary stress is on syllables two and four away from primary stress: gúmbulgàban 'turkey', bàluwáa 'slowly'.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive (CVV heavy), unbounded: every long vowel (and vowel+glide sequences, which count as long) takes stress, even in adjacent syllables; with no long vowel, primary stress is initial; secondary stress alternates two and four syllables from the primary. Giacon adds first-hand refinements from the tapes: verb-final -Vy takes final stress (gubí-y, bumá-y), purposive forms of trisyllabic short-vowel stems often shift stress to the second syllable (bumáligù, wanaˈgigu), and some suffixed/reduplicated words (Gàmilaráay, màrrgamarrgáay) violate the rules; he flags word stress as 'not well described' (p.453). This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'weight' coding from Williams 1980 and refines it (VG/VGV count as heavy; purposive and -Vy exceptions). It does not supersede Williams 1980, which Giacon explicitly cites as the source of the rules and which was written from work with living speakers; Giacon 2017 is the corroborating newer reference grammar.

new_statements.relation_note: Identical in substance (nearly verbatim) to the existing Giacon 2017 sec 2.9 statement already held by the project: same three rules, same exceptions. Confirms the weight-sensitive coding; note the catalog_records entry printed for this item has an empty rule field, so this thesis (with Giacon 2017) is the citable source for the weight-sensitive rule. Giacon attributes the rules to Williams (1980: 27) and Austin (1993a), i.e. they are secondary here.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded weight-sensitive stress: every long vowel (CVV; vowel+glide and vowel+glide+vowel sequences count as long) is stressed, even in adjacent syllables; if the word has no long vowel, primary stress is on the first syllable. Giacon prefaces the rules with 'The acoustic realisation of stress has not been measured instrumentally, so the degree to which it is realised by pitch, loudness or length is not known' (p. 507).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rule 3, p. 508: 'Secondary stress is on syllables two and four away from primary stress: gúmbulgàban "turkey", bàluwáa "slowly".' Because of this, stress depends on stem length: búmaldànha 'is hitting' vs gímubìldanha 'is making'.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 508: verbs with final -Vy stress the last syllable (gubí-y 'swim-FUT', bumá-y 'hit-PST') while other tenses of the same verbs are initial (gúbi-nyi, búma-li); some purposive forms of trisyllabic short-vowel stems shift stress to the second syllable (bumáligù, not complying with rule 2; wanaˈgigu; 'a similar change in stress is found in WN'); some suffixed and reduplicated words break the rules: Gàmilaráay ('or perhaps equal stress on the first and last syllable'), màrrgamarrgáay 'trapdoor spider'. 'The area awaits further study.' Ch. 15 (conclusions) adds 'Word stress is not well described'.
new_statements.identity_note: Giacon 2014 describes Yuwaalaraay (YR) and Gamilaraay (GR) together as 'YG' and gives one set of stress rules for both, noting a similar purposive-stress shift in Wangaaybuwan (WN). Reid 2010's examples are labelled Gamilaraay. Smyth 1878 vol. 2's Kamilaroi content (Ridley's appendix) is ethnographic, not linguistic. Poetsch & Lowe 2010 and Jones, Chandler & Lowe 2010 are about NSW revitalisation programs generally, not about this language in particular.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Gamilaraay is predictable from the phonological shape of words and can be assigned by rule. We need three basic principles, two applying to primary stress and one to secondary stress: PRIMARY STRESS 1. assign primary stress to long vowels. When a word contains two long vowels in adjacent syllables then both are stressed equally. ... 2. if a word contains no long vowels, assign primary stress to the vowel of the first syllable. ... SECONDARY STRESS Secondary stress is assigned to the second and fourth vowels counting backwards or forwards from the vowel which has primary stress, except that final syllables cannot not bear secondary stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and as the existing Giacon 2017 statement (long vowels stressed, else initial; alternating secondary stress). Giacon 2017/2014 explicitly names 'Austin (1993a)' together with Williams (1980:27) as the source of the stress rules, so this is the primary statement behind the catalog record rather than new evidence. It adds one detail relative to the existing statement's summary: final syllables are barred from secondary (not primary) stress. Giacon's later refinements (V+glide counting as long, verb-final -Vy stress, purposive stress shift) are not in Austin.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Predictable, quantity-sensitive, unbounded: every long vowel carries primary stress (two long vowels in adjacent syllables are both stressed equally, e.g. thiinaa [ˈDiːˈnaː], guniinii [guˈniːˈniː]; thalaa 'where' has final stress [Daˈlaː]); a word with no long vowel has primary stress on the first syllable (mara, bumali, thulumay). The result is a regular alternating pattern in polysyllables (S-U-S-U or U-S-U-S in four-syllable words).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress falls on the second and fourth vowels counted backwards or forwards from the primary-stressed vowel, except that a final syllable cannot bear secondary stress (gaarrumali [gàːrumàli-type], ngandabaa [ŋàndabáː], galinggalii [gàliŋgalíː]).
new_statements.exceptions: Austin remarks that equal stress on adjacent long-vowel syllables 'would appear to be an unusual characteristic for an Australian language'. The comitative -(b)araay has its first a shortened or elided after disyllabic roots (gamil-araay [gàmɪl(ə)ráːi]), which he links to the preferred S-U-S pattern since the long vowel of -araay carries primary stress (citing Ridley 1875:4 on 'Kamilaroi'). No lexical exceptions to the placement rules are listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Austin 1993 describes Gamilaraay (Kamilaroi) proper of north-central NSW, reconstituted largely from older records plus Austin's and Wurm's field notes, with comparative notes on Yuwaalaraay/Yuwaaliyaay (Williams 1980). The target record is keyed gami1243 but named 'Yuwaalaraay'; Glottolog gami1243 is Gamilaraay, and the catalog/Giacon treat Yuwaalaraay and Gamilaraay together, with the same stress rules stated for both.

tone.quote: Gamilaraay Yuwaalaraay has patterns for stressing or emphasising parts of a word. The stressed part of the word is emphasised or said a bit louder, and maybe for a bit longer. ... This is a preliminary discussion of the sound patterns of GY phrases and sentences. The area needs more research. As a very general observation, much GY talk consists of short phrases, whereas English talk tends to have longer sections of continuous sound, and more variation in volume.
